Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
34-year-old male with 6-week history of generalized fatigue, myalgias, and prior transient calf rash; Lyme disease considered.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Persistent tiredness and aching “all over” for ~6 weeks (since late Jan/early Feb, 2 wks after U.S. hiking holiday).  
• Associated symptoms: Mild ↓ appetite; no weight loss; no fevers recalled except possible low-grade with sore throat; no cough, SOB, GI, GU, or neuro symptoms; no joint swelling.  
• Skin: Single oval rash on posterior calf mid-/late-Feb; minimally pruritic; resolved over ~2 wks. No current rashes.  
• PMH: Asthma, hay fever.  
• Medications: Preventive asthma inhaler (morning & night – dose/route/frequency not fully documented); OTC antihistamine (name/dose not documented).  
• Allergies: Not discussed.  
• Social: Non-smoker; occasional alcohol; lives with wife; works in health technology; reduced exercise due to fatigue.  
• Travel: Active outdoor holiday in the United States immediately before symptom onset.

Examination:
• No examination performed/recorded.  
• Vitals not documented.

Impression:
• Unexplained fatigue and myalgias ×6 weeks; prior resolving calf rash suggestive of possible erythema migrans → rule out Lyme disease.  
• Differential includes viral/post-viral fatigue and other systemic causes (to be evaluated with baseline labs).

Plan:
• Arrange blood tests: CBC, renal, liver function, thyroid, inflammatory markers, and Lyme serology.  
• If Lyme test positive, commence appropriate antibiotic therapy.  
• Patient to book phlebotomy via support line.  
• Telephone follow-up ~1 week after labs to review results and management.  
• Advise patient to seek earlier review if symptoms worsen (not explicitly documented but customary – NOT added).

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements: Allergy status, detailed medication list (names/doses), family history, occupational exposures, vitals, physical exam.  
● No explicit contradictions noted.  
● Transcript quality: Generally clear; minor dropouts but clinically sufficient.
